item.title: Richard Lingeman, Cultural Historian and Biographer, Dies at 95
item.description:
Richard Lingeman, a magazine editor who wrote an acclaimed study of small-town America and biographies of Theodore Dreiser and Sinclair Lewis that helped revive interest in those once-towering American novelists, died on July 5 in Manhattan. He was 95.

His death, at a hospital, was confirmed by his daughter, Jenifer Lingeman. He lived on the Upper West Side.

As a journalist, Mr. Lingeman had an eclectic career. In the late 1950s, he and Victor S. Navasky founded the satirical magazine Monocle. He went on to serve as an editor at The New York Times Book Review and, in 1978, was named executive editor of The Nation, the left-leaning political magazine then led by Mr. Navasky.

After 18 years as executive editor, Mr. Lingeman stepped down to become a senior editor at the magazine, a position that gave him more time to write books.

His most notable early work, “Small Town America: A Narrative History 1620-the Present” (1980), examined the development and decline of American towns, from the earliest Puritan settlements to the Midwestern trading centers and the cow towns and mining camps of the West.

Incorporating observations from authors like Mark Twain, Sherwood Anderson, Booth Tarkington, Edgar Lee Masters and Willa Cather, Mr. Lingeman showed readers what they might find in a Midwestern general store; how railroads filled countless towns with European immigrants; and how the industrial revolution bore down on those towns, spelling obsolescence for many small farmers and craftsmen.

The book was not a sentimental portrait of neighborly communities where residents gather around a piano in the parlor and eat peach ice cream in summertime. “Small Town America,” the critic John Leonard wrote in The New York Times, presented a world of “authoritarians and conformists, speculators and real-estate sharpies, absentee landlords and vigilantes, bankers without enough money and railroad entrepreneurs with too much money, bribery and racism and false fronts and a class system as oppressive as anything to be found in old Europe.”

Mr. Lingeman branched into biography with two volumes devoted to Mr. Dreiser, a fellow Hoosier whose early 20th-century novels “Sister Carrie” and “An American Tragedy” were initially denounced as blasphemous and obscene for plotlines that included premarital sex and premeditated murder.

Mr. Dreiser’s works often featured ruthless working-class social climbers and took readers to unrefined environs like flophouses and factories. They came to be regarded as contemporary classics, in part for bringing a new kind of realism to the exploration of class and the American success story.

In “Theodore Dreiser: At the Gates of the City, 1871-1907” (1986) and “Theodore Dreiser: An American Journey, 1908-1945” (1990), Mr. Lingeman praised Mr. Dreiser for his role in elevating American literature.

“Out of his passions, contradictions and suffering,” Mr. Lingeman wrote in the second volume, noting Mr. Dreiser’s bouts of debilitating melancholy and volatile romantic affairs, “he wrenched the art that was his salvation from the hungers and depressions that racked him.”

The novelist Cynthia Ozick, reviewing the first volume in The Times, complained that the biography did not sufficiently strive to resolve the great Dreiser riddle: How could “a workhorse daily journalist” possibly “transform himself into a novelist of such encompassing, gritty, recalcitrant power”?

Yet the writer and literary critic Alfred Kazin, also writing in The Times, called the complete work “a fascinating documentation of the most troubled life led by any important modern American writer.”

After his works on Mr. Dreiser, Mr. Lingeman pursued another biography — of Sinclair Lewis, a Minnesotan who was the first American writer to win the Nobel Prize in Literature and whose novels, set in the Midwest — including “Main Street,” “Elmer Gantry” and “Babbitt” — concerned conformity, provincialism, middle-class materialism, hucksterism and hypocrisy.

“Sinclair Lewis: Rebel From Main Street” (2002) was part of Mr. Lingeman’s lifelong pursuit to “understand the role of the small town in American history,” he said. It also attempted to repair Mr. Lewis’s reputation after Mark Schorer’s exhaustive 1961 biography, “Sinclair Lewis: An American Life,” seemed to Lewis admirers to unduly emphasize the author’s personal failings.

“It rather depressed me,” Mr. Lingeman said of the earlier biography in a 1995 interview with the Sinclair Lewis Society Newsletter. “I think Schorer showed a failure of sympathy, at times a simmering hostility, to both the man and his works, that now seems excessive.”

Allowing that “Lewis’s life was often sad and self-destructive,” he also noted that Mr. Schorer had overlooked what a first-tier satirist and political and social critic Mr. Lewis was: “He was a funny man, as well as a trenchant critic of American flaws, which he knew as well as a rejected lover knows his mistress’s body.”

By the time Mr. Lewis died in 1951, his literary style had fallen out of favor. Mr. Lingeman’s sensitive portrait, which highlighted Mr. Lewis’s intelligence and insight into human frailty, spurred a rethinking of his influence, especially in works like “Ann Vickers” and “Kingsblood Royal” that touched on feminism and race.

Writing in The Los Angeles Times, the author Keith Taylor called Mr. Lingeman’s book “the most important re-evaluation of Lewis in more than a generation,” adding that he demonstrated convincingly that Mr. Lewis had influenced writers as varied as Richard Wright and John Updike.

Richard Roberts Lingeman was born on Jan. 2, 1931, in Crawfordsville, Ind., about 50 miles northwest of Indianapolis. He was the younger of two sons of Byron Lingeman, an eye, ear, nose and throat doctor, and Vera (Spencer) Lingeman, who managed the home.

At Haverford College, near Philadelphia, he majored in sociology and minored in American literature. In college, he told the C-SPAN host Brian Lamb in 2002, he was surrounded by Eastern prep school graduates “who seemed somehow to my naïve eye to be suaver and more cultured.” Writing a biographical study of Mr. Lewis for his senior thesis, he said, was his way of developing his own “sense of identity” as a Midwesterner.

After graduating in 1953, he spent three years in the Army and was assigned to the counterintelligence corps, which he called “an appalling hotbed of McCarthyism.” He was also sent to Japan, he said, to spy on ultranationalist groups.

Following his discharge, he attended Yale Law School and quickly realized he was not cut out to practice law. During that time, he started Monocle with Mr. Navasky, a fellow law student. The first parody that Mr. Lingeman wrote was of T.S. Eliot’s poem “The Waste Land.”

Mr. Navasky raised the money to publish Monocle as a “leisurely quarterly” and set up shop in New York City, where it attracted contributors like the cartoonist Edward Sorel and the humorists Calvin Trillin and Dan Greenburg. It saw a brief swell of attention during the 1963 newspaper strike, when it produced parody issues of The New York Post and The Daily News under the names The Pest and The Daily Noose. But it could never quite establish itself on a sound financial footing.

Mr. Lingeman freelanced for other publications and wrote two books, about prescription drugs (“Drugs From A to Z,” 1969) and America’s home front during World War II (“Don’t You Know There’s a War On?,” 1970).

In 1969, he joined The Times Book Review, where he remained for nine years, assigning reviews and compiling a weekly column of publishing news, “Book Ends,” before Mr. Navasky recruited him to serve as the executive editor of The Nation.

Mr. Lingeman married Anthea Nicholson, a British graphic designer, in 1965. In addition to his daughter, she survives him.

His last book, published in 2012, was “The Noir Forties,” an examination of how a moody and often cynical film genre that flourished after World War II reflected the anxieties of battle-scarred veterans, a repressive political period and the Cold War in an atomic age.

Ash Wu contributed reporting.

item.title: Palestinian Americans File Discrimination Lawsuit Against Columbia
item.description:
Five Palestinian Americans, who include a professor, a former professor, a student and two former students at Columbia, filed a lawsuit against the university on Monday, claiming it helped to foster a hostile and discriminatory environment on campus following the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack against Israel.

The complaint, filed in New York State Supreme Court, is the latest lawsuit in a series of ongoing legal battles over Columbia’s handling of campus speech, safety and discipline following the attack and during the subsequent war in Gaza.

The lawsuit comes a little more than a year after the university agreed to pay a $200 million fine to settle federal allegations claiming it had failed to do enough to protect Jewish students from antisemitism.

“Columbia has discriminated against its students, faculty and staff who are of Palestinian origin through its failure to adequately protect its community members from harassment by others, and indeed, actively encouraged such harassment,” the complaint reads.

Kimberly Winston, a spokeswoman for the university, declined to comment on Tuesday, citing the pending litigation. Jonathan Wallace and Rihan Issa, the lawyers listed for the five plaintiffs, did not respond to emails or phone calls.

Though the complaint mentions Columbia faculty and staff members, university administrators and affiliated student groups, it focuses on the university’s Office of Institutional Equity, which describes itself on its website as a “centralized resource for addressing all reports of discrimination and discriminatory harassment.”

Columbia’s leadership has described the creation of the office in August 2024 as an essential step in combating antisemitism and restoring order in the wake of campus protests against the war in Gaza.

The plaintiffs argue that the office routinely investigated Palestinian students and staff members based on a definition of antisemitism promoted by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance, which lawyers for the plaintiffs argue conflates antisemitism with criticism of Israel.

As a result, the lawsuit says, the office investigated students and university employees for participating in pro-Palestinian protests and or wearing kaffiyehs to class.

At the same time, according to the complaint, the office did not adequately look into complaints of harassment against Palestinian students and faculty members.

“In stark contrast to the O.I.E.’s aggressive investigation of complaints alleging antisemitism based on protected Palestinian advocacy, Columbia systematically failed to investigate complaints submitted by its Palestinian community members,” the complaint says, referring to the Office of Institutional Equity. “The O.I.E. rarely acknowledged receipt of such complaints, and when it did, it failed to take any follow-up action.”

In the lawsuit, the plaintiffs describe instances in which they say they were “doxxed,” physically attacked or surveilled in the immediate aftermath of the 2023 attacks and during the subsequent protests on Columbia’s campus.

While attending the university as a graduate student in 2024, one plaintiff, Layla Saliba, was attacked with a foul-smelling chemical substance during a campus protest that January.

Ms. Saliba said she received no institutional support, and the university later paid a $395,000 settlement to the student perpetrator, who sued after being suspended. (In his lawsuit, the student said he had used a nontoxic “fart” spray.)

In the complaint, a former full-time lecturer claims she was threatened by a university physician and doxxed, forcing her to resign before her contract expired. Several plaintiffs say they developed anxiety and other mental health issues because of the harassment.

The lawsuit presents Shai Davidai, a former Columbia professor, as a ringleader of the doxxing campaigns. Mr. Davidai has routinely posted online about former colleagues who support a Palestinian state.

Mr. Davidai said in a statement on Tuesday that the lawsuit was “lie-riddled,” “anti-Israeli” and “anti-American.” He is not listed as a defendant in the suit.

“I have never doxxed anyone, and I never would,” Mr. Davidai wrote in an email.

The plaintiffs, who are seeking a jury trial and damages, believe Columbia violated both state and city human rights laws.

“Rather than fulfill its legal obligations to remediate the hostile environment,” the complaint says, “Columbia actively participated in and amplified the racially, ethnically and politically motivated targeting of Palestinian students, staff and faculty.”

item.title: Trump Sues New York and Other States Over In-State Tuition for Migrants
item.description:
The Justice Department on Monday sued three states — Connecticut, New York and Vermont — over policies that offer in-state tuition to undocumented immigrants at public colleges and universities.

The lawsuits argue that the policies are unconstitutional, violate federal law and discriminate against U.S. citizens from other states who pay thousands of dollars more in out-of-state tuition.

The legal actions were the latest effort by the Trump administration to tighten immigration enforcement and crack down on policies it sees as favoring immigrants who do not have legal status at the expense of Americans.

“Congress long ago made clear that states cannot put illegal aliens over our nation’s own citizens,” Stanley Woodward, the associate attorney general, said in a statement. “By granting illegal aliens in-state tuition, New York, Vermont and Connecticut are doing just that. No more.”

In New York, undocumented students who graduated from a state high school pay $7,700 a year at State University of New York campuses, while citizens from other states are charged about $17,730.

Emma Wallner, a spokeswoman for Gov. Kathy Hochul of New York, said that the state was reviewing the lawsuit but expressed confidence that the state’s policies would be upheld.

“In keeping with the law, the governor believes all New York high school students deserve the opportunity to pursue higher education in the state,” she said in a statement.

William Tong, the attorney general in Connecticut, addressed President Trump in a statement: “How we run our schools and teach our kids is none of your business, and you have no authority to force the sovereign state of Connecticut to deny our kids a future.”

He added that Connecticut offered in-state tuition and financial aid to all eligible students because “all kids deserve the opportunity to learn, to advance and to achieve their dreams.”

The office of Vermont’s governor, Phil Scott, did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

The Trump administration has now filed lawsuits against 17 states challenging in-state tuition for undocumented residents, the Justice Department said in a news release on Monday, including against California, New Jersey and Virginia.

The results have been mixed.

States with friendly Republican leadership — including Nebraska, Oklahoma and Texas — have chosen not to oppose the Trump administration, instead reaching settlements with the federal government to end the tuition policies.

The Justice Department secured a major legal victory in Illinois, where a federal judge struck down the state’s tuition laws as unconstitutional last month. But, a federal judge in Minnesota handed the Trump administration a defeat in March after dismissing a similar lawsuit filed against that state, a decision that the Justice Department is appealing.

Under a federal law passed in 1996, states that provide in-state tuition to undocumented immigrants based on state residence must offer that same tuition rate to all citizens in the United States.

“This is a simple matter of federal law: Colleges cannot provide benefits to illegal aliens that they do not provide to U.S. citizens,” Brett A. Shumate, the assistant attorney general in the civil division of the Justice Department, said in a statement.

In New York, undocumented immigrants can receive in-state tuition if they attended a local high school for at least two years and graduated and applied to college within five years of graduating — similar to Minnesota, where three years of local high school are required. Connecticut and Vermont also condition in-state tuition on the completion of local high school.

While the Justice Department argued that this acts as an indirect residency requirement, a federal judge in Minnesota ruled that the tuition benefit complies with federal law because it is tied to high school attendance rather than state residence.

Lawsuits in other states are pending, but the issue could reach the Supreme Court if lower courts are split.
